headline: Supreme Court Directs Bar Council To Issue 'Official Protest Permits' On Stamped Parchment Before Allowing Dissent
body:
The Supreme Court has issued a landmark directive ordering the Bar Council to replace its arbitrary disciplinary actions against law students with a standardized, bureaucratic 'Permit to Express Dissent' system. Under the new guidelines, any student wishing to demonstrate on campus must first file an affidavit of their grievances on a ₹500 non-judicial stamp paper, which will then be subject to a three-week review process by a panel of retired stenographers.

'Protest is a fundamental right, but it is currently being exercised with a distressing lack of administrative oversight,' noted a senior judicial spokesperson while unveiling the new application form. 'By requiring students to list their protest slogans in triplicate and obtain a no-objection certificate from their hostel warden, we ensure that dissent remains orderly, predictable, and fully compliant with the legacy filing systems of the colonial era.'

Legal experts have lauded the move, noting that it successfully balances the constitutional right to dissent with the judiciary's deeper, more primal desire for mountains of paperwork. The Bar Council has reportedly already begun drafting a 'Standard Operating Procedure for Peaceful Assembly,' which will include a mandatory dress code and a designated three-by-three-foot square for all future campus agitation.

Students who fail to secure the stamped permit prior to raising a placard will be subject to a nominal fine, payable exclusively through a physical treasury challan submitted in person at the local district court. The court noted that it hopes this will finally teach the youth that the only thing more powerful than a movement is a correctly processed application form.
caption: The court has finally brought some much-needed red tape to the messy world of student activism. Nothing says 'upholding democracy' like requiring a triplicate form for your freedom of speech. #LawLife #Bureaucracy #StudentProtest #Judiciary (satire)

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Index 0 perfectly captures the bureaucratic absurdity of Indian institutions by treating protest as a regulated administrative process. The specific, deadpan details—such as the 'three-week review by a panel of retired stenographers' and the 'non-judicial stamp paper'—create a brilliant, grounded satire that feels authentically biting compared to the more whimsical concepts in the other entries.
